extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military commanders, convening authorities, and military legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Authoritative guidance on the jurisdictional limits, procedural powers, and pleading/evidence practices of courts-martial under the Articles of War, for use by military legal officers and commanders. Covers who is amenable to court-martial, pleadings, presence/attendance, evidence after pleas, and courtroom conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating of members must follow convening order
rubrics_metrics.description: A general court-martial has no authority to seat members in any order of rank different from that indicated by the convening order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members must be seated in the order specified by the convening authority; deviations are unauthorized (C. 15262, Sept. 8, 1903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may not arrest its judge advocate
rubrics_metrics.description: For the court or the president of the court to place or order the judge advocate in arrest would be an unauthorized proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While contempt proceedings under Article 86 might be appropriate in proper cases, arrest or punishment of the judge advocate can only be imposed through the convening authority or other competent commander (R. 3, 603; R. 21, 629).

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority over accused's person except when before court
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has no authority over the person of an accused except when he is before it; it cannot arrest him or by its own order cause him to be brought to the place of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compelling attendance and arrest are duties of the convening officer or post commander; lack of arrest does not bar valid proceedings if jurisdiction otherwise attaches (R. 22, 606; R. 39, 44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court cannot assign counsel or compel an officer to act as counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: A military court has no authority to assign counsel to an accused unprovided with counsel, and has no power to compel an officer to act as counsel for an accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nor can the court excuse one of its members to enable him to act as counsel for an accused (R. 13, 400; R. 35, 440; P. 57, 417).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may seek attendance of uncalled parties via judge advocate or convening authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court-martial desires the testimony of a party not introduced by either side, it may call upon the judge advocate to have such party summoned or apply to the convening authority/post commander to have him ordered to testify, and may adjourn for a reasonable time to await attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court may adjourn the trial for a reasonable time for attendance; this applies especially to military persons who must be ordered before the court (R. 25, 578).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegrams are not privileged; subpoenas can compel telegraph operator and dispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial (by subpoena duces tecum, through the judge advocate) may summon a telegraph operator to appear and bring a certain telegraphic dispatch; telegrams are not privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telegraphic dispatches are admissible evidence and may be compelled (P. 31, 149; C. 20085).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may not arrest witnesses for false swearing; must report to convening authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has no authority, as such, to arrest or require its judge advocate to arrest a witness suspected of false swearing upon a trial; it should report the facts to the convening authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper course is to report suspected false swearing for action by convening authority (B. 3, 109).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts-martial are courts of limited, statutory jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts-martial are bodies of exceptional and restricted powers; their cognizance is confined to the distinctive classes of offenses recognized by the military code; their jurisdiction is criminal and they cannot adjudge damages for personal injuries or other civil rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may not rescind contracts or pass upon civil rights; they are created by statute for the limited purpose of awarding punishment for military offenses (B. 27, 454; 0. 3608; 11196; 17768).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts-martial cannot be used to collect private debts
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial cannot be availed of for the collection of private debts of officers and can take no notice of their financial obligations except as evidence of fraud or dishonor when admissible in proof of an offense under the Articles of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private financial disputes are outside military criminal jurisdiction (P. 35, 463).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirements for jurisdiction must be strictly followed
rubrics_metrics.description: As the origin and authority of the court-martial are statutory, the statutes must be closely followed and no presumption can be made in favor of the court's jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and convening authorities must not assume jurisdiction beyond statutory grant (K. 55, 486).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military jurisdiction attaches if prosecution commenced before enlistment expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who has not in fact been discharged may be brought to trial after his term of service has expired provided that before expiration proceedings with a view to trial (arrest or service of formal charges) were duly commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest or formal charges prior to expiration attach military jurisdiction and permit lawful trial and punishment thereafter (R. 26, 512; multiple authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge not effective until notice; soldier remains amenable until notice delivered
rubrics_metrics.description: If a discharge does not take effect until notice thereof (actual or constructive), a soldier who commits an offense on the day he was to be dishonorably discharged but before the discharge was delivered is amenable to military jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of delivery/notice determines effective separation for jurisdictional purposes (P. 27, 383).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deserter prosecution date relates to confinement under charge
rubrics_metrics.description: A military prosecution of a deserter is instituted when he is confined under a charge of desertion; in case of civil criminal proceedings, priority in prosecution relates to that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confinement under charge fixes the institution date for military prosecution (C. U042).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction and abandonment principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an offense is triable in civil (territorial) courts and also by court-martial under particular articles, the offender may be tried in the territorial court; but upon abandonment of civilian prosecution the jurisdiction of a general court-martial will attach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: murder on a military reservation in a Territory — territorial courts may try; if civilian prosecution abandoned, military jurisdiction attaches (C. 20902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loose, indefinite charges; plead specifics when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Loose and indefinite forms of charge such as 'fraud,' 'worthlessness,' 'inefficiency,' 'habitual drunkenness,' etc., should be avoided, though they may be sustained when accompanied by specifications setting forth actual military neglects or disorders as equivalents to 'conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleaders should draft specific specifications; general wording may suffice only when concrete particulars are alleged (R. 19, 280; R. 28, 253).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific offense requires specification of constituent facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specific offense (an offense under an article other than the general — sixty-second — article) is charged and the specification does not state facts constituting that offense, the pleading will be insufficient as to that specific offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, charge plus specification taken together may amount to an allegation under the general article; consistency between charge and specification is required (R. 11, 491; R. 15, 680; R. 16, 551).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest is not essential to jurisdiction; voluntary appearance suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: An arrest, though usually preliminary, is not essential to a military trial; it is sufficient if the accused voluntarily appears or in obedience to an order submits himself to trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to be formally arrested, or prior release without rearrest, is not a bar to trial or ground for invalidating proceedings or sentence (R. 2, 77; R. 17, 419; C. 8982).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons in service amenable while under arrest awaiting trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in the military service are amenable to the jurisdiction of courts-martial for military offenses committed by them while in arrest or confinement awaiting trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confinement pending trial does not remove military amenability (P. 33, 335).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension from rank does not remove military jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspension from rank does not affect the officer's right to his office; he retains it and remains subject to military control and to jurisdiction of a court-martial for offenses committed pending the term of suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies whether suspension imposed by sentence or by commutation; officer remains amenable during suspension (R. 30, 157; R. 38, 221; C. 17277).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension status equivalent whether sentence-imposed or commuted
rubrics_metrics.description: The status of an officer under suspension is the same whether such suspension has been imposed directly by sentence or by way of commutation of a more severe punishment; he remains amenable to trial for offenses committed pending suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commuted dismissal to suspension does not shield from subsequent court-martial (R. 38, 221).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilians entitled to jury trial; military jurisdiction limited in peacetime
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Sixth Amendment civilians are guaranteed the right to trial by jury in all criminal prosecutions; in time of peace a court-martial cannot assume jurisdiction over an offense committed by a civilian without violating the Constitution — only in war and exceptional circumstances may civilians be amenable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military jurisdiction over civilians in peace is unconstitutional; exceptions limited and narrowly construed (R. 19, 475; R. 38, 641; C. 17901).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutes attempting to give military jurisdiction over civilians in peace are unconstitutional
rubrics_metrics.description: Any statute attempting to give jurisdiction over civilians in time of peace to military courts is unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited holdings supporting the constitutional principle (R. 42, 250; C. 20120; C. 17901).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service must be legally complete for military amenability
rubrics_metrics.description: To become amenable to military jurisdiction an officer or soldier must have been legally and fully admitted into the military service of the United States; persons appointed by a state governor but not mustered into U.S. service are not amenable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission/mustering into U.S. service is prerequisite to military jurisdiction (R. 12, 475; C. 4294).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military jurisdiction over civilians limited to those who have subjected themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has no jurisdiction over a civilian in peacetime who has not subjected himself to military jurisdiction by entering the Army; jurisdiction in peace is exercisable only over those who have entered the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: civilian assaulting high military official in peace is not triable by court-martial (C. 11210).

rubrics_metrics.name: Act conferring jurisdiction over prisoners limited in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of June 18, 1898 gave jurisdiction to general courts-martial over prisoners during confinement as such, but was not intended to make other changes in existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute should not be construed to expand military jurisdiction beyond its intended limited effect (G. 5589; G. 10003; G. 13926; G. 16220).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation or separation of victim does not deprive court of cognizance
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that before trial an officer who was the victim of an injury has resigned or been separated from the Army cannot affect the authority of a court-martial to take cognizance of the military offense involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction over the offense persists despite subsequent separation of injured officer (R. 32, 623).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of accused to be present; waiver and counsel representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused has a right to be present during all material proceedings of his trial but may waive that right; if he absents himself the court may continue proceedings and reach findings/sentence. If the accused has counsel, the court may allow counsel to continue presentation of the case, including evidence and argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waiver of presence does not vitiate proceedings; courts may permit counsel to proceed in accused's absence (R. 24, 488; R. 11, 260 and 295; C. 14767; C. 21787; C. 23941).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arraignment before court-martial bars state court jurisdiction while proceedings pending
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an officer or enlisted man has been arraigned before a duly constituted court-martial for an offense legally triable by it, the jurisdiction thus attached cannot be set aside by a state court — state court jurisdiction is for the time suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offender may, however, be voluntarily surrendered by the United States to civil authorities (P. 8, 484).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation from service generally ends amenability for prior offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or soldier (except as otherwise provided in the sixtieth article) ceases to be amenable to military jurisdiction for offenses committed while in service after he has been separated by resignation, dismissal, muster out, discharge, etc., and thus become a civilian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many authorities support the rule; statutory exceptions (sixtieth article) must be observed (R. 1, 395; R. 2, 49; C. 14389).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of resignation/discharge before discovery bars later trial for undiscovered offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who, by acceptance of resignation, dismissal, discharge, etc., has become wholly detached from military service cannot be made liable to trial by court-martial for offenses committed while in the service on the ground that such offenses were not discovered until after he had left the army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation cuts off amenability for pre-separation offenses discovered later (R. 37, 374).

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to service does not revive lapsed jurisdiction for prior offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Returning by a dismissed or separated officer or soldier to the service does not revive jurisdiction for offenses committed while in the service which had lapsed upon separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior offenses that lapsed upon separation remain not subject to later court-martial upon reenlistment (R. 5, 314; C. 22840).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of honorable/discharge on amenability for desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: An honorable discharge ends the particular contract/term of enlistment but does not relieve the soldier from consequences of a desertion committed during a prior enlistment; similarly for discharge without honor. A dishonorable discharge by sentence is punitive and covers all unexpired enlistments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorable/other discharges release from amenability for offenses charged within the particular term to which they relate except as provided in the sixtieth article; dishonorable discharges as punishment do not permit later amenability for prior desertion except as provided statutorily (P. 49, 442; C. 2115; P. 53, 179).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of control to execute sentence does not confer jurisdiction over prior offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention of military control over a dishonorably discharged soldier for execution of sentence does not confer military jurisdiction over offenses that may have been committed by him prior to his separation; he is held as a general prisoner, not as a soldier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1898 act conferring jurisdiction over general prisoners did not change this rule (R. 31, 34; C. 7762; C. 9406).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible trial of officers for misconduct as cadets
rubrics_metrics.description: There is ground for the view that a prosecution may be instituted against an officer for an offense committed while a cadet, as cadets are not discharged upon graduation but may be promoted, so no hiatus in military status appears to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No clear precedent but statutory/functional continuity of status supports potential prosecution (C. 22475).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial generally controls its own procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial should generally be left to determine its own course of procedure, except where defined by law, regulation, or usage; a commander may not require a court to adopt a certain procedure on matters within its discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders may recommend practices but cannot prescribe procedure (R. 34, 138). Example: cannot order courts to take testimony in guilty-plea cases though may recommend it.

rubrics_metrics.name: No prohibition on sitting on Sunday
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law prohibiting a U.S. court-martial from sitting on Sunday, and a sentence adjudged on that day is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity unaffected by the weekday of sitting (R. 39, 321; C. 2955; C. 15591).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may sit with doors closed in discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial is authorized, in its discretion, to sit with doors closed to the public; however, courts in this country are almost invariably open, except temporarily for deliberation or in scandalous cases where closure may be recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary trials are public; closure reserved for special circumstances (R. 29, 34; C. 1637; G. C. M. Record No. 55974).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may take up a new, brief case when trial suspended
rubrics_metrics.description: After entering upon a trial which must be suspended due to absence of material witnesses or other cause, a court-martial is authorized, in its discretion, to take up a new case unlikely to involve extended investigation and proceed to termination before resuming the first trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows efficient use of court time; discretion should be exercised with regard to complexity of the substitute case (R. 8, 281; R. 9, 650; R. 26, 548).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate charges for several distinct offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the act committed involves several distinct offenses, the accused may properly be arraigned upon the same number of separate charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count and charge each distinct offense separately (R. 30, 489).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may allow withdrawal or change of pleas in discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial is authorized, in its discretion, to permit an accused to withdraw a plea of not guilty and substitute guilty, and vice versa, or to substitute a special plea; applications should be allowed when in good faith, not for delay, and when not resulting in unreasonable prolongation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should generally consent to plea changes made in good faith (R. 30, 672).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matters of evidence are not proper subjects of plea
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and circumstances that are properly matters of evidence (e.g., extenuating circumstances) are not legitimate subjects of pleas and should be offered in evidence rather than pleaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: good conduct in battle after the offense cannot be pleaded; personal hostility behind a charge is evidence, not a plea (R. 6, 79; R. 34, 554).

rubrics_metrics.name: If accused unable to plead due to intoxication, enter not guilty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an accused declined to plead on the ground of being so much under the influence of liquor that he could not remember what occurred, the court properly directed a plea of 'not guilty' to be entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects accused's rights when mental state prevents intelligent plea (R. 29, 545).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirability of taking evidence even when plea is guilty
rubrics_metrics.description: While a commander cannot order courts-martial to refuse guilty pleas or to take evidence regardless of pleas, it is proper and generally desirable—especially for enlisted men or where specifications are vague—that the prosecution introduce evidence even when a guilty plea is entered, so the court and reviewing authority can appreciate the nature of the offense and properly estimate punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence after a guilty plea aids sentencing, review, and recommendations; particularly important where sentences are mandatory or in capital cases; lack of evidence in deserter guilty-plea cases is often problematic (R. 3, 667; R. 6, 370; R. 29, 124; C. 5093).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused must be given opportunity to present rebuttal/character evidence after prosecution introduces evidence post-plea
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is introduced by the prosecution after a plea of guilty, the accused should be afforded an opportunity to offer rebutting evidence or character evidence if he desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures fairness and opportunity to mitigate or rebut the prosecution's showing (R. 13, 423).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider plea together with any statement or confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, in connection with a guilty plea, the accused interposes a statement or confession (oral or written), both plea and statement should be considered together; if the statement suggests evidence exists that will constitute a defense or relieve culpability, the court should call upon the judge advocate to obtain and introduce such evidence if practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must evaluate plea and statement jointly and pursue any indicated exculpatory evidence (R. 14, 585; R. 26, 562; R. 28, 123; R. 29, 11, 348).

rubrics_metrics.name: An inconsistent statement may control over a guilty plea
rubrics_metrics.description: If an accused pleads guilty but immediately makes an oral statement inconsistent with the plea, and no evidence is introduced, the statement rather than the plea should be regarded as the intelligent act; the court should counsel or direct entry of a not guilty plea and proceed to trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the judge advocate should introduce proof as under an ordinary not-guilty plea (R. 8, 274; R. 17, 48; R. 30, 33; P. 61, 394).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional allowance of testimony after case formally closed but before finding
rubrics_metrics.description: In the interests of justice, the court may in its discretion allow introduction by either side of material testimony after the case has been formally closed but before a finding has been reached, provided the party shows good reason for not producing it earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such allowance must be exceptional and justified; evidence introduced at this late stage requires good excuse for prior omission (R. 12, 401; R. 17, 398; R. 31, 35).
